links.outcome: Whether clinician reviewers detect harmful or inaccurate AI outputs
links.effect: Specialists were five times more likely than residents to rate responses harmless; post hoc analysis showed specialists may disregard conflicting or inaccurate information. Fewer than two-fifths of responses were deemed harmless.
links.quote: Post hoc analysis revealed that specialists may inadvertently disregard conflicting or inaccurate information in their assessments.

links.outcome: Human vulnerability to failing to detect incorrect or harmful AI outputs
links.effect: Specialists rated responses higher than resident trainees in all domains (p < 0.001) and were five times more likely to consider responses harmless, indicating vulnerabilities in safeguarding against harmful outputs.
links.quote: In our analysis, we have demonstrated disconcerting human vulnerabilities in safeguarding against potentially harmful outputs, which seemed to be most apparent among experienced specialists.

links.outcome: Comparative performance of candidate LLM chatbots on the same clinical scenarios
links.effect: GPT-4.0 had higher composite scores than Gemini Pro (p = 0.001) and Claude 2 (p = 0.006), and was better on factual consistency, comprehensiveness, and absence of harm.
links.quote: Analysis showed that GPT-4.0 achieved significantly higher composite scores compared to Gemini Pro (p = 0.001) and Claude 2 (p = 0.006).

screen.reason: The study evaluates the performance and perceived safety/harmfulness of four LLMs across clinical infectious disease scenarios using blinded reviews by specialists and residents, but does not test an organizational deployment practice or guardrail intervention.
